newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Traders see more weakness in Thai offshore debt.
newsitem.headline: Traders see more weakness in Thai offshore debt.

text.p: The outlook continues to look grim for Thai dollar-denominated debt paper traded offshore as the country's financial woes continue unabated, traders said.
"For top-tier banks, five-year paper denominated in U.S. dollars probably will widen by a further five to 10 basis points," a trader said.
Spreads on Thai paper traded in the secondary market have widened significantly over the last few months as Thailand grapples with a currency crisis that has wreaked havoc with its financial markets.
For example, Thai Farmers Bank paper due in 2002 is currently trading at 58 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate compared with only 28 basis points in January.

Thai Farmers Bank is one of Thailand's top-tier institutions. Like a number of Thai banks, it was downgraded by Moody's Investors Services to A3 from A2 after the rating agency cut Thailand's sovereign rating.
Moody's cut Thailand to A3 from A2 in April.
The Kingdom of Thailand launched a Yankee bond into the U.S. market shortly after the downgrade with an issue that was widely praised as being correctly priced in a difficult market.
The 10-year bond was priced to yield 90 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
The bond's price has drifted since then, however, and dealers said the issue was trading at about 97 basis points over the benchmark on Wednesday.
Traders said weakness in the Thai bonds was likely to continue.
"It is too early to tell whether the Thai economy has bottomed, and a further rating downgrade within this year is not impossible," a U.S. investment banker said.
"At the moment, there is almost no bid for Thai paper in the secondary market," a trader at European bank said.
Conditions might deteriorate if Thai banks' bad loan situation turns out to be even worse than anticipated, the European trader added.

Bond investors have turned away from Thailand because of the country's general economic malaise, but traders said the central bank's efforts to combat speculation against the baht are having more direct effects on Thai companies hoping to raise funds through debt.

Moves by the Bank of Thailand to restrict foreigner's access to baht has made it extremely difficult for foreigners to invest in baht-denominated corporate bonds, helping dry up the pool of investors in baht paper.
As a result, Thai companies have had to offer higher yields on their baht-denominated paper to attract local investors.
With baht financing increasingly expensive, cash-hungry finance firms are expected to borrow offshore in U.S. dollars, adding more supply to a market that is sated with Thai paper.
"Thai banks would have to pay even more to attract foreign investors," a banker said.
Recently, attempts by Thai issuers to tap offshore markets have proven difficult.
For example, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand earlier this month cancelled an issue that already was in syndication after its counterparty rating was cut by Standard and Poor's Corp.
On Tuesday, Thailand's state-run property support agency Property Loan Management Organisation (PLMO) said it would seek government permission to raise funds in foreign markets.
But analysts said they did not expect PLMO bonds to attract a strong response.
